newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal banks seen forced back to basics in EMU.
newsitem.headline: Portugal banks seen forced back to basics in EMU.

text.p: Portuguese banks will be forced to rely almost entirely on the traditional business of lending for their living if Portugal gets into the single currency, leading bankers and analysts say.

The lucrative commissions that banks earn from foreign exchange and bond trading will become a thing of the past when the escudo is swallowed up inside the euro, the single currency the European Union plans to launch in January 1999.

"There will be no more 'market-makers' in escudos and it is unlikely that we will be able to take on this role in euro from the start," said Miguel Beleza, economic adviser to the board at Banco Comercial Portugues and former Bank of Portugal governor.

The loss in income will be significant. According to the 1995 annual report of the Portuguese Banking Association, domestic banks earned some 80 billion escudos ($506 million) of net profit from financial operations that year.

A senior official at one leading Portuguese bank, who asked not to be named, said he calculated that the banking system could lose around half this amount in annual trading income as a result of the switch to the single currency.

"The banking sector is a loser (with the single currency)...even if it can gain in the medium and long term from the better economic health of its clients," said Rui Martins dos Santos, chief economist at Banco Portugues de Investimento.
"We are going to go back to traditional banking after all the risk management activity," he added.

Financial markets have become increasingly confident that Portugal, which has made qualifying for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) its top policy priority, will pass the stiff economic tests for entry.
Analysts and bankers said that one consequence of the loss of earnings from commissions would be that banks would probably have to start charging for services that are now provided free.
"Charge for the effect cost of deposits, of cheques and electronic banking? I think that it is inevitable," said Beleza.

The Portuguese Banking Association (APB) has set up under the auspices of the central bank working groups to examine various aspects of the move to a single currency -- the interbank market, treasury operations, payments and accounting, legal aspects and the relationship between clients and banks.
But the commissions are only discussion bodies and banking officials admit that in practical terms little has yet been done to prepare banks for the big change.
To a large extent, this reflects a lack of clear instructions from Brussels on steps to be taken, bankers say.
"No clear programme of transition to the single currency has yet been given to us. It would be excellent if it had, but it has not," APB president Joao Salgueiro told Reuters.
Salgueiro said that the only things that had been really spelled out -- beyond the January 1, 1999 start-up date -- were the name and the denominations of the future euro bank notes.
"But other countries are no better off...they don't know any more than us," he added.
Despite the upheaval to be brought about by the virtual disappearance of foreign exchange trade, bankers said that it was too early to say whether there would be a big impact on bank employment.
"There will be a cut in foreign exchange activity but there could be be developments in other areas," said Salgueiro.
